stories.headline: PLA’s patrolling behaviour keeps LAC disturbed, Govt. says
stories.title: PLA’s patrolling behaviour keeps LAC disturbed, Govt. says
stories.summary: MEA says “Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns”; video of ITBP chief’s remarks on situation in Arunachal Pradesh removed after The Hindu’s report on the border situation; Congress slams government for suppressing information
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Line of Actual Control (LAC) has been “disturbed” by the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) patrolling behaviour, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Friday (October 23, 2026) in response to questions about a report in The Hindu on skirmishes along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh.
The report, which had quoted the outgoing Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border.
Police Forces (ITBP), Shatrujeet Kapur, expressing concern over “face-offs” underway since July 2026, drew sharp criticism from the Congress.
Despite the Ministry’s confirmation, the video of Mr. Kapur’s speech, given at an event in Alwar on Thursday (October 22, 2026), was deleted from the ITBP’s official YouTube channel.

This was the first time the government has officially accepted that, more than two years after Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping announced a détente between their militaries, the border areas remain tense and “get disturbed” over patrolling routes.

“As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns,” Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told journalists at a briefing here, blaming the PLA for the divergences.

“Both sides continue to use existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation along the Line of Actual Control,” he added, directing queries on the specific situation to the Ministry of Defence.

Mr. Jaiswal also reiterated the government’s position since the beginning of the four-year military standoff at the LAC, including the Galwan clashes in 2020, that the “maintenance of peace and tranquility in the border areas is essential for the overall development of bilateral relations”, and said that both sides were in touch about improving their understanding of the LAC for “better border management”.
In a post on X, Mr. Kharge said the confirmation by the chief of ITBP forces stationed at the LAC was “deeply alarming”.
The Congress chief alleged that Mr. Modi’s June 2020 statement that no one had entered Indian territory after the Galwan clashes had emboldened China.

Addressing a press conference, Congress media and publicity department chairman, Pawan Khera, commended the ITBP’s ‘Shaurya Commandos’ for handling the confrontations with China, but accused the government of suppressing information from the border.

“The fact that China has entered our territory does not bother [the government]; what bothers them is that this has been reported,” Mr. Khera said, adding that “image is more important for them than the country’s interests”.

stories.headline: Rajasthan High Court Admits Appeal Against SC/ST Ward Reservation Over Allegedly Fake Population Data, But Refuses To Stay Election Process
stories.title: Rajasthan High Court Admits Appeal Against SC/ST Ward Reservation Over Allegedly Fake Population Data, But Refuses To Stay Election Process
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Rajasthan High Court has admitted an appeal challenging the reservation of wards in Gram Panchayat Majhiwala for persons belonging to Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs), allegedly based on incorrect population data, but refused to stay the ongoing Panchayat election process.
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Sanjay K. Agrawal and Justice Baljinder Singh Sandhu declined...
an affordable subscription scheme!!!

The Division Bench of Chief Justice Sanjay K. Agrawal and Justice Baljinder Singh Sandhu declined to interfere with the election process, observing that the State Election Commission had published the election programme for Rajasthan's Panchayat elections on October 3, 2026, thereby setting the process in motion.
Article 243-O of the Constitution restricts judicial interference in electoral matters relating to Panchayats, with the objective of preventing disruption of the election process.
The petitioner challenged the reservation of wards in Gram Panchayat Majhiwala for SC/ST candidates, alleging that the population figures used for the reservation were incorrect.
He contended that there were only 14 voters belonging to the Scheduled category in the Gram Panchayat and, therefore, the reservation ought not to have been made.
The petitioner also challenged the notification concerning the reservation of the Sarpanch post for Panchayat Samiti Majhiwala.
A Single Judge dismissed the writ petition as not maintainable in view of Article 243-O, since the election programme had already been published.
The petitioner subsequently filed a special appeal before the Division Bench.

The petitioner argued that the election programme was issued on October 3, 2026, but the election notification contemplated under Rule 23 of the Rajasthan Panchayat Raj Election Rules, 1994, had not yet been issued.
Therefore, he contended, the constitutional bar under Article 243-O was not attracted.

stories.headline: A new era of leadership: Visionaries, innovators and changemakers
stories.title: A new era of leadership: Visionaries, innovators and changemakers
stories.summary: The future is shaped by individuals who look beyond established boundaries, challenge conventional thinking and turn their knowledge into meaningful action. Across industries, leadership is taking new forms, driven by innovation, specialised expertise, personal conviction and a growing focus on creating lasting value.From entrepreneurship, healthcare and taxation to education, art, mental wellness, spirituality and child rights, today's changemakers are contributing to conversations that extend beyond their immediate professions. Through their work, they are addressing evolving needs, empowering individuals, sharing knowledge and exploring new ways to create a positive impact.What connects these diverse journeys is a commitment to growth and the belief that meaningful progress begins with a clear purpose. Whether through professional excellence, creative expression, personal transformation or social responsibility, each individual brings a distinct perspective to the challenges and opportunities of the present.As industries and communities continue to evolve, their stories offer a closer look at how experience, innovation and determination can translate into action. Together, these visionaries reflect a broader understanding of success, one that values not only individual achievements but also the ideas, contributions and possibilities they bring to the world around them.Ms. Preetty G. SharmaPreetty G. Sharma, Founder of astro divine energy, is an Astrologer and spiritual guidance practitioner with over 25 years of experience, working with individuals / corporations across 30+ countries. Her approach combines astrology-based insights, spiritual practices and Divine Power to help people navigate challenges related to relationships, family, career, business, finances and personal growth. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she states that her guidance and work with Divine Power helped save lots of lives and support families through circumstances. Her mission is to connect one person in every family with Divine Power, encouraging self-awareness, lasting change, kindness and conscious living. Through her work, Preetty seeks to guide people towards a better future and success in life .Dr. Rajni RathiDr. Rajni Rathi is a Vastu and Astrology expert with over 20 years of experience in guiding individuals and organisations towards balance, harmony and purposeful growth. Her expertise combines traditional wisdom with contemporary perspectives on energy alignment, spatial harmony and the five elements. She has guided thousands of individuals and organisations, helping them understand the role of spaces, energy and balance in personal and professional environments. Recognised for her contributions to the field, she has received several national and international honours, including the Lifetime Achievement Award. She is also the owner of Würfel on MG Road, Delhi, a premium modular kitchen and wardrobe brand inspired by European design and craftsmanship.Vinod Kumar GinjalaVinod Kumar Ginjala, Founder and Managing Director of Gravita Oasis Review Solutions Pvt Ltd, focuses on strengthening U.S. home health operations through medical coding, clinical documentation review, quality assurance and technology. A Bachelor of Pharmacy graduate, he holds the Certified Professional Coder (CPC), COQS and BCHH-C certifications. He founded Gravita in 2021, drawing on his healthcare and home health coding experience. His work addresses documentation inconsistencies, strengthens review processes and supports accurate coding decisions. He is also working on AI-driven solutions for the home health sector, with a focus on making documentation and coding workflows more efficient and reliable. His vision is to combine healthcare expertise, technology and education to build practical solutions for evolving home health needs.CA Jayesh GogriCA Jayesh Gogri has specialised in indirect taxation for nearly three decades. In 2012, he co-founded GSC Intime Services, where he is Director, advising business houses on GST, customs and government incentives, now across 40+ cities in India. His firm's mantra is simple: "Solve the issue!" He and GSC received the ET Business Excellence Award 2026 from The Times Group, and he shared the BCAS Jal Erach Dastur Award for Best Feature (2025-26). He has delivered 200+ talks at forums including IIM and ICAI, and authored books including GST Margdarshika in four languages. Guided by value before fees, he is now writing a book on living joyfully despite all odds.Josephine M DiasJosephine M Dias spent 29+ years as an educator at St Thomas' Girls School, Delhi, before reinventing herself after retirement. After competing at 59, she became VG Mrs India Empress 2nd Runner-Up 2025 and joined VG Pageants as a team member, guiding women from different backgrounds through their pageant journeys. A certified health coach shaped by her own transformation journey, she wrote OMG! Don't Try Adventure With Your Health, which champions Medicine 3.0 and prevention before cure. She also holds the Magnetic Personality Award in public speaking from Sneh Desai and works with AstoneaOne. Her message: listen to your body when it whispers, it shouldn't have to scream to get your attention.RiyaaRiyaa is a fine artist known for statement paintings and custom portraits, trained at European art institutes. Her work has been exhibited in Paris, Berlin, Florence, London, Delhi and Mumbai, and she counts global HNIs, CEOs, VPs and politicians among her clients. She won a Bronze medal at the All India Mandala contest. As Founder of Riyaa dartstudio and Color Caastle Art Academy, she teaches that fundamentals set creativity free. She is the author of The Portrait Atelier, a three-part series on drawing the human figure, with books on acrylics, watercolour and colour theory on the way. Her belief is simple: anyone can learn art, one fundamental at a time.Krishna RavalKrishna Raval began as an engineer and Bharatanatyam dancer, then built a career in a multinational manufacturing company while earning an MBA in Operations. A lifelong quest to understand herself led to a new path as an author and certified life coach. Krishna's book, 'Feelings, Freakouts, Figuring It Out: A Teen's Playbook to Ditching the Script', speaks to young adults trying to work out where life is headed. Also a contributor to the ICA anthology, she helps people change limiting beliefs and build lives that truly resonate with them. A lifelong learner, she explores everything from languages and spirituality to the ever-evolving world of AI. She believes everyone has a story worth telling and deserves a space where they feel safe, heard, and accepted without judgment.Dr. Kunti NagwekarDr. Kunti Nagwekar is an educationist and corporate trainer who has taught Eye Yoga since 1996. After 27 years as a lecturer in Mumbai, she founded Sampoorna Wellbeing Technology and earned a PhD in "Mind and Vision." Her Creative Visualisation courses have reached corporates, business owners, the Armed Forces and film personalities. A full-time Sevak with MaitriBodh Parivaar, she wrote My Divine Talks To Me! in 36 days. It won recognition from the International Council of Authors and sold 160 copies in eight days, by word of mouth. Its message is simple: the Divine lives in your heart, as your closest friend. Her next book is Eye Care for You.Padmaa Priyaa K.RPadmaa Priyaa K.R is the founder of Gaaya The Mother, a Tarot reader and coach, space and energy healer, tarot artist and author. Her work weaves together Tarot, space alchemy, numerology, art and writing, helping women who have spent years putting themselves last reconnect with their voice. A teacher at heart, she specialises in reading Tarot through symbols and even shows students how to hand-make their own decks. She is the author of The Humans We Forgot to Become and created Tattva Tarot: The Path to Your Soul, a 108-card deck and companion book rooted in Sanskrit words and Indian culture. Her vision: a community where women learn, create and lead.Adv. Juhi DamodarAdv. Juhi Damodar is a legal professional practising since 1998, beginning at the Mumbai High Court, Maharashtra and Goa Bench, and now Chairperson of the Child Welfare Committee, Udupi. A TEDx Speaker and recipient of the Global Women in Business and Leadership Award 2025, she wrote Justice for Every Child, a practical guide to the POCSO Act, 2012 that blends law, psychology and rehabilitation, covered by ANI, The Tribune and others. Known for her work on child rights and third-party parental alienation, she also speaks on public health and law at the ECIPH Dialogue. Her aim: law that keeps pace with lived realities and gives every child a stronger voice.Together, these ten journeys show that leadership today is not defined by a single industry, title or path. It is defined by the willingness to keep learning, to create with courage and to serve with purpose. As the world continues to change, the people featured here are a reminder that the future belongs to those who turn insight into action and ideas into impact, and who, in doing so, open the door for others to follow.The pages slugged ‘Brand Connect’ are equivalent to advertisements and are not written and produced by Forbes India journalists.

stories.headline: When practical short-term action meets long-term strategic thinking
stories.title: When practical short-term action meets long-term strategic thinking
stories.summary: In a quarter century of public service, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has demonstrated an extraordinary ability to link practical short-term action with long-term strategic thinking. In that spirit, my review of Indian economic performance over the same period has two goals. The first is to identify intrinsic strengths of the economy that have revealed themselves in our long-term performance. The second is to assess how these might guide policy in the critical period that lies ahead.Growing EconomyTo me, a striking fact is that the Indian economy has grown at an average rate of 6 percent between the start of this century until Covid hit in 2020. These data (based on national sources) are the basis of published detailed long-term analysis by, among others, the World Bank. They are the best we have for a fast changing, growing economy where, of necessity, reality outpaces measurement.There are other successes of recent Indian experience, including low inflation, reduction in absolute poverty (measured in terms of personal consumption) and declining consumption inequality, but here my focus is on growth, as ultimately, it is sustained economic growth that makes these other achievements affordable.Also Read: When households became shareholders: The quiet story of India's balance sheetSustained economic growth over a long horizon is not unprecedented in global post-war economic experience. This was the case in some countries now classified as high-income (Japan, South Korea) and those still on their way, most notably China. Even so, India’s growth achievement remains significant.Measured economic growth of any economy (such as the recent print of 7.8 percent annual growth for the first quarter of FY27) is determined by the interaction between aggregate supply and aggregate demand. Particularly in the richer economies and increasingly in India, short-term fluctuations in aggregate demand drive measured growth. Such demand fluctuations occur along an arc defined by the supply side of the economy.Sustained growth of aggregate supply reflects the steady accumulation of the most basic inputs (the ‘factors of production’: Capital and labour but also environmental inputs such as land and water). Labour includes demographic and behavioural factors (such as the willingness or ability of women to seek employment), and, crucially, improved health and better education (human capital).Classical economic theory proposes a ‘law of diminishing returns’, where the application of each marginal unit of these factors generates a lower return. In a democracy, this principle is reinforced by electoral compulsions. Accumulation of either physical or human capital implies deferred consumption. If undertaken by government, this implies taxation or increased debt. For all these reasons, the most important but also most elusive factor in sustaining long-term growth is innovation in the way these factors are used, commonly called technical progress, or, more geekily, growth in ‘total factor productivity’, TFP growth in short.In an ideal world we would have authoritative studies of the sources of Indian growth divided between factor accumulation (what the economist Paul Krugman has called ‘perspiration’) and TFP growth (‘inspiration’). Despite heroic efforts by the Reserve Bank of India to put out consistent data to support such analysis, I have not been able to come up with many recent studies of economy-wide growth in India’s TFP. China is an economy that has continued to devote vast resources to investment but is paying the price both in low shares of consumption and diminishing returns to capital formation.Also Read: Can the Indian economy grow fast even as prices rise?The US is a country whose extraordinarily steady GDP growth of 2 percent per year for almost a century has been much studied, in an environment where the underlying data have, at least until recently, been above reproach. Indeed, the formalisation of growth theory and the focus on TFP came out of an attempt to explain the US growth record despite indifferent investment rates. My reading of that literature is that the steadiness reflects the institutional flexibility of a vastly more affluent country than India today. And it is noteworthy that that this long-run steadiness has been maintained through war and peace, boom and slump.Flexible GovernanceWhat conclusions do I draw from India’s past record, based upon the US experience on the one hand, and the Chinese experience on the other? And what guidance does India’s past provide for our choices in future?On the first, the 25-year record suggests that the economic management framework (political and administrative) India had achieved by 2000—50 years after becoming a republic (and nine years after cautious embrace of global markets)—has proved resilient to shocks, including the one we are currently experiencing. My own recent experience in government suggests that there is deep underlying political consensus on a mixed economy and on social protection which may inhibit radical change.On the second question I would offer a series of observations. First, 50 years is probably a better horizon for both planning and assessing social and economic transformation. We are today half-way toward the prime minister’s aspiration of a modern, empowered society in 2047, something that crucially depends on sustained economic growth.Second, it would be a fatal mistake to assume that, despite the past record, steady 6 percent growth is assured. It is not, and we are where we are only because our style of governance has proven to be flexible. We are still not affluent enough to worry about the middle-income trap, but we are fortunate to have a large pool of current and prospective workers so that labour availability will not be a constraining factor for the coming decade.My final thought, derived from the discussion earlier, is that our policy focus should be less on sectors and more on factors of production: Labour, land and capital. We have not succeeded in top-down industrial policy in the past. There is little reason to think we will do better in the future. We are a more balanced economy than China and every bit as entrepreneurial as the US. opening: In a quarter century of public service, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has demonstrated an extraordinary ability to link practical short-term action with long-term strategic thinking.
In that spirit, my review of Indian economic performance over the same period has two goals.
body: The first is to identify intrinsic strengths of the economy that have revealed themselves in our long-term performance.
The second is to assess how these might guide policy in the critical period that lies ahead.
Growing EconomyTo me, a striking fact is that the Indian economy has grown at an average rate of 6 percent between the start of this century until Covid hit in 2020.
These data (based on national sources) are the basis of published detailed long-term analysis by, among others, the World Bank.
They are the best we have for a fast changing, growing economy where, of necessity, reality outpaces measurement.

There are other successes of recent Indian experience, including low inflation, reduction in absolute poverty (measured in terms of personal consumption) and declining consumption inequality, but here my focus is on growth, as ultimately, it is sustained economic growth that makes these other achievements affordable.
Sustained economic growth over a long horizon is not unprecedented in global post-war economic experience.
This was the case in some countries now classified as high-income (Japan, South Korea) and those still on their way, most notably China.
Even so, India’s growth achievement remains significant.
Particularly in the richer economies and increasingly in India, short-term fluctuations in aggregate demand drive measured growth.
Such demand fluctuations occur along an arc defined by the supply side of the economy.
Sustained growth of aggregate supply reflects the steady accumulation of the most basic inputs (the ‘factors of production’: Capital and labour but also environmental inputs such as land and water).
Labour includes demographic and behavioural factors (such as the willingness or ability of women to seek employment), and, crucially, improved health and better education (human capital).
Classical economic theory proposes a ‘law of diminishing returns’, where the application of each marginal unit of these factors generates a lower return.
In a democracy, this principle is reinforced by electoral compulsions.
Accumulation of either physical or human capital implies deferred consumption.
If undertaken by government, this implies taxation or increased debt.

For all these reasons, the most important but also most elusive factor in sustaining long-term growth is innovation in the way these factors are used, commonly called technical progress, or, more geekily, growth in ‘total factor productivity’, TFP growth in short.

In an ideal world we would have authoritative studies of the sources of Indian growth divided between factor accumulation (what the economist Paul Krugman has called ‘perspiration’) and TFP growth (‘inspiration’).

Despite heroic efforts by the Reserve Bank of India to put out consistent data to support such analysis, I have not been able to come up with many recent studies of economy-wide growth in India’s TFP.
China is an economy that has continued to devote vast resources to investment but is paying the price both in low shares of consumption and diminishing returns to capital formation..
Indeed, the formalisation of growth theory and the focus on TFP came out of an attempt to explain the US growth record despite indifferent investment rates.
My reading of that literature is that the steadiness reflects the institutional flexibility of a vastly more affluent country than India today.
And it is noteworthy that this long-run steadiness has been maintained through war and peace, boom and slump.
Flexible Governance.
What conclusions do I draw from India’s past record, based upon the US experience on the one hand, and the Chinese experience on the other?
And what guidance does India’s past provide for our choices in future?

On the first, the 25-year record suggests that the economic management framework (political and administrative) India had achieved by 2000—50 years after becoming a republic (and nine years after cautious embrace of global markets)—has proved resilient to shocks, including the one we are currently experiencing.
My own recent experience in government suggests that there is deep underlying political consensus on a mixed economy and on social protection which may inhibit radical change.
On the second question.
I would offer a series of observations.
First, 50 years is probably a better horizon for both planning and assessing social and economic transformation.
We are today half-way toward the prime minister’s aspiration of a modern, empowered society in 2047, something that crucially depends on sustained economic growth.
Second, it would be a fatal mistake to assume that, despite the past record, steady 6 percent growth is assured.
It is not, and we are where we are only because our style of governance has proven to be flexible.

We are still not affluent enough to worry about the middle-income trap, but we are fortunate to have a large pool of current and prospective workers so that labour availability will not be a constraining factor for the coming decade.
My final thought, derived from the discussion earlier, is that our policy focus should be less on sectors and more on factors of production: Labour, land and capital.
We have not succeeded in top-down industrial policy in the past.
There is little reason to think we will do better in the future.
We are a more balanced economy than China and every bit as entrepreneurial as the US.
We should take comfort from the fruits of past liberalisation and trust the genius of our population to make the best of the new opportunities that technology offers.

stories.summary: In a final order issued on Friday, the market regulator directed ASTAPL and its founder Avadhut Dinkar Sathe to disgorge and refund ₹546.17 crore to eligible investors and participants who paid for its unregistered services.
reasons: source: event has 4 copies, primary source counted once

article_sentences: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has imposed penalties totalling ₹11.5 crore on Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy Pvt.
Ltd (ASTAPL) and its directors, and barred them from accessing the securities markets for periods of up to two years for providing unregistered investment advisory and research analyst activities.

In a final order issued on Friday, the market regulator directed ASTAPL and its founder Avadhut Dinkar Sathe to disgorge and refund ₹546.17 crore to eligible investors and participants who paid for its unregistered services.
It has also ordered a deposit of ₹67.87 crore in interest with Sebi’s Investor Protection and Education Fund.
Sebi imposed a penalty of ₹6 crore on ASTAPL, ₹4 crore on Sathe and ₹1.5 crore on Gouri Avadhut Sathe, another director.

Sebi also prohibited ASTAPL and Avadhut Sathe from accessing or dealing in the securities markets, directly or indirectly, for two years or until they comply with the refund direction, whichever is later.
Gouri Sathe has been barred for six months.
Sebi had issued an interim order on the matter on 5 December 2025.

The regulator’s action follows its findings that the academy’s activities went beyond financial education and included investment advice and research-related services without the required registrations.
The order cites recommendations on specific securities, including buy and sell calls, price targets and stop-loss levels, delivered through live sessions and WhatsApp communications.
The order directs ASTAPL and Sathe to publish refund notices within 30 days of receiving it in two national newspapers—one English and one Hindi—and a local-language newspaper.
The notices must explain how eligible claimants can seek refunds.

stories.headline: India’s bulk Scotch tariff dispute risks undermining India-UK trade deal, industry group says
stories.title: India’s bulk Scotch tariff dispute risks undermining India-UK trade deal, industry group says
stories.summary: An industry association has sought urgent clarification from the government as the tariff dispute raises concerns over market access and investment
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from a reduced 75% tariff goes against provisions agreed in an India-UK trade deal, a group representing liquor makers Diageo and Pernod Ricard wrote in a letter seen by Reuters.

Whisky tariffs were a sticking point during the years of protracted negotiations leading up to the deal's July 15 implementation, though India ultimately agreed to halve import taxes on certain Scotch imports from 150% to 75% immediately and to 40% over 10 years.
The British government said "iconic UK products" like whiskies would benefit from the pact.

Indian investigators, however, have privately told companies the reduced rate does not apply to bulk Scotch concentrates, creating the first significant dispute over the free trade agreement since it took effect.

India's Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod and Diageo and questioned executives this month as part of an investigation into whether they misclassified imported products to benefit from the reduced rate.

In a letter to the commerce minister on Friday, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India (ISWAI) wrote that the classification issue "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom."
"The preferential tariff treatment negotiated...
could effectively become unavailable for these imports," continued the letter, a copy of which was seen by Reuters.
ISWAI declined to comment on its letter, while India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond.
Pernod, which counts India as its biggest market by volume, declined to comment, and Diageo did not respond to a request for comment.
Both told Reuters earlier this week that they were cooperating with Indian authorities carrying out the investigation.
Import tariff disputes have long been a sore point for foreign investors in India, who have in the past faced demands for large amounts of back-tax.

stories.headline: Cabinet Sub-Committee seeks to draw up department-wise plan to tackle El Nino induced drought conditions
stories.title: Cabinet Sub-Committee seeks to draw up department-wise plan to tackle El Nino induced drought conditions
stories.summary: 358 mandals provisionally identified as drought-affected based on rainfall, crop coverage
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Cabinet Sub-Committee on Drought and El Nino conditions chaired by Deputy Chief Minister M. Bhatti Vikramarka on Friday resolved to prepare a comprehensive and department-wise action plan to tackle the drought caused by El Nino conditions.

The plans will focus on safeguarding supply of water for drinking and irrigation and ensuring uninterrupted electricity, agricultural support and rural employment so that people do not face hardships in the coming days.

The first meeting of the Cabinet Sub-Committee, constituted to review the drought and El Nino situation in the State and recommend appropriate measures to the government, was held here on Friday (October 23).
The meeting primarily discussed the impact of El Nino and drought in various parts of the State, water availability, relief measures for farmers and future action plans.

Sub-Committee members and Ministers N. Uttam Kumar Reddy, Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy, D. Seethakka, Tummala Nageswara Rao and Vakiti Srihari along with Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju and secretaries of the concerned departments attended the meeting.
Mr. Vikramarka asked the officials to scientifically assess drought conditions and examine the mandals eligible for declaration as drought-affected areas under the prescribed guidelines.
He stressed that the government’s priority was to minimise the impact of drought and ensure timely delivery of necessary assistance to people through coordinated efforts.
He instructed officials to assess not only areas already experiencing severe drought but also mandals where the drought impact exceeds 20%.
An advance assessment of the likely impact of drought on various sectors would help the government provide timely assistance to those in need, he said.
He suggested that every department identify the challenges and prepare a clear action plan to address them.
He asked the officials to anticipate challenges in the power sector arising from El Nino conditions and take measures in advance.
Mr. Uttam Kumar Reddy asked the District Collectors to conduct weekly review meetings with the officials concerned to monitor the measures being implemented to address the drought conditions.

stories.headline: Former Radio Kashmir Director Bashir Arif appointed to Muslim Personal Law Board J&K
stories.title: Former Radio Kashmir Director Bashir Arif appointed to Muslim Personal Law Board J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 23: Veteran broadcaster, poet and former Director of Radio Kashmir Srinagar, Bashir Arif, has been appointed as a member of the Muslim Personal Law Board Jammu and Kashmir, along with six other members. Arif, who also served as Deputy Director General of All India Radio, is a prominent figure in Kashmir's broadcasting and literary circles. He has contributed to Kashmiri radio, television, theatre and literature over several decades. According to an order issued by the Board, the appointments were made in consultation with Chairman Mufti Nasir-ul-Islam Farooqi, Vice Chairman Syed Mohammad Aslam Andrabi, General Secretary Prof M Yaseen Kirmani and the Executive Committee. Besides Arif, the newly appointed members include Mushtaq Ahmed Pandow, Molvi Abdul Lateef Wani, Mufti Mushtaq Ahmed Kambay, Mufti Umer Qasmi, Gulzar Ahmed Charloo and Syed Muzamil Rizvi. Mufti Umer Qasmi has been inducted as a youth member, while Gulzar Ahmed Charloo and Syed Muzamil Rizvi have been appointed as members representing social activism. The Board said the appointments were aimed at strengthening its organisational structure and expanding efforts to safeguard Muslim Personal Law, promote religious and social welfare and address issues concerning the Muslim community across Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh. The order was issued by Er Danish Reshi, Advisor to the Grand Mufti of Jammu and Kashmir and General Secretary (Organisation) of the Board. All seven appointments have come into effect immediately.

stories.headline: Supreme Court holds voters can prosecute candidates for concealing information
stories.title: Supreme Court holds voters can prosecute candidates for concealing information
stories.summary: The judgment by a Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu said the law does not insist that only public servants or competent authorities were eligible to lodge complaints against electoral candidates
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has held in a judgment that ordinary private citizens can file criminal complaints against candidates for giving false information or concealing information while filing their nomination papers for an election.

The judgment by a Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu said the law does not insist that only public servants or competent authorities were eligible to lodge complaints against electoral candidates.

The court’s judgment empowers the vigilant citizen-voter with the locus standi to directly act against dishonesty in electoral politics, and ensure transparency in polls right from the stage of filing nominations.
Candidates have to file personal affidavits along with their nominations.
Senior advocate Sanjay Nuli, who appeared in the case, pointed out that these affidavits were part of legislative efforts to maintain the purity of elections and a healthy democracy.
Voters must be educated and well-informed about the contesting candidates, including the latter’s assets, educational qualifications and criminal antecedents.
Concealing personal information or filing false details to hoodwink the voters was a non-cognisable and bailable offence under Section 125-A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
The Section provides that a guilty party would be liable to face imprisonment for six months, fine or both.

Justice Datta interpreted that the rigour of Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), that only a complaint lodged by a public servant must be taken cognisance of by a court of law, did not affect Section 125-A of the 1951 Act.

“If indeed it were the intention of the legislature that cognisance of any offence relating to the furnishing of false information by a candidate in an affidavit with intent of being elected in an election could only be taken if the complainant were a public servant, the same could have been provided by an amendment of Section 195 CrPC,” the court noted.
Section 125-A was inserted into the 1951 Act in August 2002.
Although the legislature was presumably aware of Section 125-A when it amended Section 195 in April 2006, it did not stipulate that the restrictions of Section 195 should apply to Section 125-A.

stories.title: ‘Monitor geopolitics closely, remain prepared to respond to immediate challenges’: Rajnath to Army Commanders
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 23: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh has exhorted the Army Commanders to closely monitor geopolitical as well as regional developments and remain prepared for future challenges. Addressing the Army Commanders’ Conference in New Delhi on October 23, 2026, he emphasised the need for a long-term strategic vision spanning the next 20-30 years, and called upon the senior leadership of the Indian Army to remain equally prepared to respond to immediate and emerging challenges. He stressed that strategies must remain dynamic and flexible, enabling timely adjustments to changing circumstances. Commending the Defence Forces for adapting to evolving operational circumstances, Rajnath Singh highlighted that innovative thinking, enhanced synergy and superior coordination, complemented by advanced weaponry, contributed to the success of Operation Sindoor. The operation sent a clear message that India would not hesitate to take necessary measures to safeguard its national interests, he said. Defence Minister appreciated the military’s restructuring efforts, with a special focus on the use of drones and modern technology. He stressed the need to strengthen capabilities, continuously assess performance, and implement necessary improvements in line with evolving circumstances. He underscored the importance of accelerating efforts in areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, data analytics, cybersecurity, and secure communication networks. Rajnath Singh emphasised that despite growing significance of challenges across the air, maritime, space and cyber domains, land warfare and ground forces would remain indispensable. He called for an integrated approach to modern warfare, stressing that success would depend on multi-domain capabilities and seamless coordination in joint operations. Defence Minister acknowledged the self-reliance efforts of the defence forces, stating that India’s growing defence manufacturing capabilities are a result of concerted efforts of all stakeholders. “Amidst the changing global landscape, Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led Government is prioritising Aatmanirbharta in defence. In the financial year 2025-26, defence production surged to a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore, with defence exports reaching an all-time high of approx. Rs 38,000 crore,” he said. Referring to the ‘Year of Reforms - 2025’, Rajnath Singh stated that reform is a continuous process, the success of which depends on effective implementation. He urged the Commanders to drive these reforms forward within their respective commands and echelons, while ensuring that they translate into tangible benefits for operational capabilities. Defence Minister credited the valour, discipline, preparedness and restraint of the Defence Forces, along with the dynamic leadership and diplomatic efforts of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, for strengthening India’s global standing. He urged the Defence Forces to maintain their focus on self-reliance, effective implementation of reforms, improved manpower management, greater participation of women and an integrated approach to national security. On the occasion, Defence Minister released the Land Warfare Doctrine, which provides an overarching framework to prepare the Indian Army to meet the challenges posed by the evolving character of warfare and future conflicts. He also unveiled the annual United Nations Journal and felicitated Indian Army personnel who have made notable contributions while serving as United Nations peacekeepers, recognising their exemplary service, professionalism and contribution to international peace and security. MoS Defence Sanjay Seth, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani, Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh and other senior officials were present on the occasion. With its comprehensive agenda, the conference has been organised to provide an important forum for the senior leadership of the Indian Army to review ongoing initiatives, identify future thrust areas and formulate appropriate policy directions towards building a progressive, adaptive, technologically enabled and future-ready Indian Army.

stories.title: Delhi BJP questions AAP on CM Mann’s goods on which he was forced to pay customs duty, fine

article_sentences: “People of the country and Punjab want Arvind Kejriwal to explain why Bhagwant Mann violated customs rules and what taxable goods he was allegedly trying to evade tax on,” said Malhotra.

New Delhi: Delhi BJP President Harsh Malhotra on Friday criticised Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann’s failed bid to evade customs duty while returning to the country after a foreign visit and asked Arvind Kejriwal to share details of the goods for which the former was penalised by the customs.

The Delhi BJP President said Mann was often in the news for allegedly setting several records by entering Parliament and the Assembly after consuming alcohol, but now he has become the first Chief Minister in the country to be fined Rs 50,000 under the Customs Act, 1962.

The Delhi BJP President drew the attention of Aam Aadmi Party Convenor Arvind Kejriwal to reports according to which Mann, while returning from a foreign trip, allegedly attempted to pass through the green channel despite carrying luxury taxable goods, in violation of customs rules.
However, alert customs officials stopped him, inspected his baggage, and subsequently imposed a fine of Rs 50,000 on several items, Malhotra said, quoting reports.

The Delhi BJP President said that it is beyond comprehension what message Mann wanted to convey to ordinary citizens by allegedly making an unruly attempt to pass through the green channel despite carrying taxable goods.
In another development, Delhi BJP spokesperson Praveen Shankar Kapoor hit out at the AAP for attempts to allege a scam in the “poor quality of paper” in textbooks distributed in government schools.
Kapoor said Delhi witnessed a textbook crisis for Classes 6 to 12 throughout the 11 years of AAP government’s rule.
Moreover, as soon as the Kejriwal government came to power in the Municipal Corporation in 2022, it created a shortage of textbooks there as well.

The Delhi BJP spokesperson said that records bear witness to the fact that, during Kejriwal’s 11-year rule, cases concerning the failure to provide textbooks reached the courts almost every year, and the Education Department was reprimanded on numerous occasions.

Kapoor said it was laughable that Delhi AAP convenor Saurabh Bharadwaj, a former minister in a government under whose tenure there was a textbook crisis in almost every academic session, was now raising questions about the poor quality of textbook paper.
It appears that Bharadwaj considers himself an expert capable of judging the quality of paper as well, said Kapoor.
